task: find the latest news about a specific topic (a company, a person, a sport, a technology) on a news site or aggregator (google news, apnews, reuters, bbc, espn): search for or navigate to the topic, sort by or judge recency, and open the relevant latest article; complete when a current article on the right topic is on screen. Surface pinned: news sites and aggregators. Variants: news commentary/opinion videos as the subject, and "daily news recap" videos where a person reads headlines to camera, do not belong.

tree.label: Keep up with the news
tree.note: do 1. 2 and 3 feed each other and repeat - the Feedly keepers build with 2 and then scan what accrues with 3; the Google keepers run 3 alone and keep nothing (RKSc, gyDs, xATD, vLA0), except one topic follow that reaches into 2.6 (64Vu). 4 from any list, though most lists are scanned and left - 9 stories and one video clip get opened across 14 keepers. 5 after 4 where the story is worth keeping; 4_Sv runs 5 without ever opening the story. 6 replaces 4 and 5 on the newsroom service (AE9a). 7 in the one keeper that closes the loop (v4vm).

questions.question: Does the sidebar already list a feed that covers the asked topic?
questions.why: The sidebar displays existing categories like 'Marketing' alongside a '+' icon to 'Follow New Sources', requiring a choice between current and new content streams.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally curate which specific news publications are added to your account.
questions.check: Does the sidebar already list a feed whose name matches the asked topic?
questions.say_example: You already follow <Marketing>, so I'll look there first.

children.label: Get into the news service
children.note: 1.1 or 1.2 to arrive. 1.3 to 1.5 only where an account gates the service - three Feedly keepers start mid-session and skip all of it (4_Sv, zCA3, r9X3), and every Google keeper walks in without an account. 1.6 replaces 1.4 on the newsroom service (AE9a). 1.7 where the edition matters (gyDs).

questions.question: Does a cookie consent banner or ad-blocker warning prevent you from interacting with the homepage?
questions.why: News sites frequently employ aggressive overlays that must be accepted, rejected, or bypassed before any search or navigation can occur.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to manage their privacy preferences or decide whether to disable their ad-blocker for this specific site.
questions.check: Does an overlay, cookie banner, or ad-blocker notice cover the page content?
questions.say_example: A cookie banner is covering the page. I said no to the optional ones, and we're through.

questions.question: Does the pre-loaded search on the page match the topic you asked for?
questions.why: The screen shows the Google News Timeline labs page pre-loaded with a search for 'christmas' and dates from December 2009.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to define the specific starting platform, search term, and historical timeframe for the task.
questions.check: What search term and date range is the page pre-loaded with, and does it match the asked topic?
questions.say_example: The page opened with an old search, <christmas> from <December 2009>. I'm clearing it and searching for <your topic>.

questions.question: Which search result is the official Feedly website?
questions.why: The first search result displays the URL 'https://feedly.com/', confirming it is the legitimate aggregator rather than a third-party or sponsored link.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally verify the search result URL to ensure you are accessing the authentic news platform.
questions.check: Does the top result's URL match the official site address, or is it labeled as an ad?
questions.say_example: The first result is an ad that looks like <Feedly>. The real site is just below it, so I'm using that.

children.label: Choose log in or sign up

questions.question: Do you want to log in to an existing account or create a new one?
questions.why: The homepage displays both 'GET STARTED FOR FREE' and 'LOGIN' buttons, requiring a choice based on whether you already have an account.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure the agent uses your existing account with its pre-configured news feeds rather than starting from scratch.
questions.check: Does the page show both a log-in button and a create-account button?
questions.say_example: Feedly wants an account. Do you already have one, or should I make a new one?

questions.question: Does the page offer an OPML import option?
questions.why: The screen presents options to either start a new free account or import an existing OPML file to set up your news feeds.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means the agent might create a new blank account instead of importing your existing curated news feeds.
questions.check: Does the page offer an OPML import option next to the free sign-up?
questions.say_example: Skipped the OPML import - started a normal account

questions.question: Which authentication method do you want to use to log in?
questions.why: The login modal presents multiple options like Google, Feedly, and various social accounts, requiring you to choose the one linked to your existing profile.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over which personal or third-party account is used to authenticate and access their personalized news feeds.
questions.check: Which sign-in methods does the login screen list?
questions.say_example: You can sign in with <Google>, <Apple>, or <email>. Which one is yours?

questions.question: Which Google account should you use to sign in to Feedly?
questions.why: The screen presents multiple Google accounts to continue to Feedly, and the choice determines which personalized news feed and subscriptions are accessed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to control which specific personal or work profile is associated with your news reading activity.
questions.check: Which Google accounts does the account picker list?
questions.say_example: Google is asking which account to use. I see <david.lin> and <your work one>. Which one?

questions.question: Does the sign-in form show a pre-filled username to sign in with?
questions.why: The screen displays a login panel with a pre-filled username and obscured password, requiring a decision on whether to proceed and if the session should be saved.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to manage their own login credentials and decide whether the session should be persistently saved on the device.
questions.check: Does the sign-in form show a pre-filled username?
questions.say_example: The form is already filled in for <newsroom01>. I'll sign in with that, and I won't save the login on this computer.

questions.question: What language and region does the page say the feed is set to?
questions.why: The sidebar currently displays 'English (Nigeria)', which will heavily influence the geographic focus and relevance of the news results you receive.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to specify the exact cultural and geographic context that determines which local or regional news stories are prioritized.
questions.check: What language and region does the page say the feed is set to?
questions.say_example: This feed is set to <English (Nigeria)>. That's why the headlines look off. I'm switching it to <English (United States)>.

children.label: Build the source feed
children.note: 2.1, then 2.2 or 2.3 raises candidates; 2.4 on every card, 2.5 where a sneak peek is wanted. 2.6 commits and 2.7 follows immediately - the platform will not let a follow float unfiled (2o_3); 64Vu's topic star is the exception, a follow with no filing step. 2.8 inside 2.7 when the feed is new; v4vm also runs 2.8 standalone and fills the empty feed afterward. repeat 2.2 to 2.7 per source - four in about 15 seconds (zCA3), six in a sitting (1HW8). 2.9 after any batch; 2.10 wherever the counts are on screen.

children.label: Search for a topic or source

questions.question: What is the results-language filter set to?
questions.why: The screen shows a 'Results language' dropdown with multiple options, allowing you to filter the news articles by languages like English, Spanish, or Japanese.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to specify your preferred reading language or to intentionally seek out foreign-language coverage of the topic.
questions.check: What is the results-language filter set to?
questions.say_example: Search results are set to <Spanish>. I'm switching them to <English>.

questions.question: What specific blog or source do you want to search for?
questions.why: The search bar requires you to input the exact name of the publication or topic you want to read about.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally select a trusted, niche source that aligns with your specific professional interests.
questions.check: Is the source search box empty, with no publication named in the request?
questions.say_example: What should I add to your feed? A publication name, or a topic to follow.

questions.question: Which listed category matches the asked topic?
questions.why: The screen displays various featured industries and skills, making it necessary to choose the right category to surface relevant news sources.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means losing the opportunity to browse and select a specific niche topic that perfectly aligns with your current interests.
questions.check: Which listed category matches the asked topic?
questions.say_example: Browsed the <Business> category for sources

questions.question: Which video channel in the sidebar matches the asked topic?
questions.why: The left sidebar lists multiple regional and topical video channels under Broadcast Video, requiring a choice to narrow down the news content.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means losing the ability to prioritize which specific region's news is most relevant to your current interests.
questions.check: Which video channel in the sidebar matches the asked topic?
questions.say_example: Filtered to the <Asia> video channel

questions.question: Which source should you select from the matching results?
questions.why: The screen displayed multiple matching sources with varying follower counts and posting frequencies, requiring a subjective choice.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to apply their personal taste or specific niche interest when choosing among multiple valid sources.
questions.check: Which matching sources does the results list show, with their follower counts and posting rates?
questions.say_example: Three sources match. <MediaShift> posts <4 a week>. <Journalism.co.uk> posts <daily> but has fewer readers. Which one should I follow?

questions.question: Do the recent article titles in the preview match the asked topic?
questions.why: Scanning the article titles grouped under 'TODAY' and 'YESTERDAY' helps you verify if the source consistently publishes content that matches your target topic.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally evaluate the nuance and quality of the article titles to decide if the source truly aligns with your specific interests.
questions.check: Do the recent article titles in the preview match the asked topic, and how recent are the dates?
questions.say_example: This source's recent posts are all <celebrity news>. That's off your topic, so I'll skip it.

questions.question: Does the page show a follow control for this source?
questions.why: Clicking the star icon changes the status to 'Following' and triggers a confirmation toast, altering your account's saved preferences.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over the curation of their personalized news feed if the agent autonomously follows topics.
questions.check: Does the page show a follow control for this source or topic?
questions.say_example: I'm following <MindShift> now. New posts will land in your <EdTech> feed.

questions.question: Is this result a bundle that follows multiple sources at once?
questions.why: The search results feature a 'Marketing Bundle' with a 'FOLLOW ALL' button that would add 10 sources at once, rather than requiring you to evaluate each one.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to keep their feed uncluttered by vetting each publication individually rather than accepting a bulk package.
questions.check: Is this result a bundle that follows multiple sources at once, and how many?
questions.say_example: This one is a bundle. Following it adds <10> sources in one go. Want all of them, or should I pick the good ones?

questions.question: Does the follow dropdown offer an existing feed that matches the topic?
questions.why: The dropdown menu after clicking follow requires choosing whether to organize this source into an existing category like 'Journalism' or to create a brand new feed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally organize your news sources into custom categories that match your specific reading habits.
questions.check: Does the follow dropdown offer an existing feed that matches the topic?
questions.say_example: Filed <MindShift> under the existing <EdTech> feed

questions.question: Does the modal show the intended feed title and collection?
questions.why: The modal displays the feed title and the selected collection, requiring verification before saving.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to verify and choose exactly which custom collection the topic feed is saved into.
questions.check: What feed title and collection does the confirmation modal show?
questions.say_example: The dialog wants to file <MindShift> under <Photography>. You wanted <EdTech>, so I'm fixing that first.

questions.question: Does the page ask for a name for the new feed?
questions.why: The screen provides an input field and suggestions like '+ Black women', requiring a decision on how to label the topic.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means losing the ability to organize and name your news sources according to your own personal categories.
questions.check: Does the page ask for a name for the new feed, and what does it suggest?
questions.say_example: The new feed needs a name. I'm calling it <EdTech>. Say a different name if you want one.

questions.question: Does the new feed appear in the sidebar?
questions.why: The sidebar updated to show 'EdTech' and 'MindShift' under 'FEEDS', confirming the topic was added and providing a way to access its articles.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to confirm the feed was added successfully and to choose exactly which source to view.
questions.check: Does the sidebar now list the new feed with the source under it?
questions.say_example: I followed it, but it hasn't shown up in your sidebar yet. I'm refreshing to check.

questions.question: Does the feed's unread count update correctly when you add new sources?
questions.why: Seeing the unread count immediately jump to 20 confirms that the platform successfully pulled in the latest articles from the sources you just added.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate visual reassurance that your custom feed is correctly aggregating the specific sources you care about.
questions.check: Did the feed's unread count go up after the sources were added?
questions.say_example: Unread count rose to <20> after adding the sources

children.label: Check the counts against the earlier screens

questions.question: Does each feed's unread state match the article dates shown inside it?
questions.why: The screen shows the 'Black Women in History' feed claiming you are caught up despite containing an article from yesterday, while the 'Journalism' feed immediately displays accurate unread counts.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might trust the false 'caught up' message and fail to find the latest news, whereas a human would manually check the feed to verify.
questions.check: Does each feed's unread state match the article dates shown inside it?
questions.say_example: The <Black Women in History> feed says you're all caught up. But inside there's an article from <yesterday>. The counts here can miss things.

questions.question: Does the publication frequency shown on the feed header agree with the search result?
questions.why: The feed header for MindShift states it publishes one article per month, contradicting the search result which claimed four articles per week.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might miss this contradiction and rely on inaccurate search results regarding how often the source publishes.
questions.check: Does the posting rate on the feed header match the rate shown in the earlier search results?
questions.say_example: The search said <MindShift> posts <4 articles a week>. Its own page says <once a month>. Expect fewer stories than promised.

questions.question: Do the different screens agree on the length of the video?
questions.why: The search results and title slate show a duration of 2:04, while the web player and import window show 2:09.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to catch a metadata mismatch that could indicate missing footage or technical errors.
questions.check: Does the video length shown here match the length shown on the earlier screen?
questions.say_example: One screen says the video runs <2:04>, another says <2:09>. I'll make sure the download plays to the end.

questions.question: Does the publication date on the loaded article match the date shown in the timeline?
questions.why: The timeline listed the article under December 19th, but the loaded article page shows December 20, 2009, indicating a discrepancy in the reported dates.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that the agent is accurately verifying the true publication date of the news.
questions.check: Does the date on the opened article match the date the timeline filed it under?
questions.say_example: The timeline filed this under <December 19>. The article itself says <December 20>. I'm going by the article's own date.

questions.question: Does the unread count update to reflect the article you just opened?
questions.why: The unread count for the EdTech feed dropping from 593 to 592 confirms that the system successfully registered your view of the latest article.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the visual confirmation that their reading progress is being accurately tracked by the news aggregator.
questions.check: Did the unread count drop by one after the article was opened?
questions.say_example: Unread count dropped <593> to <592> after opening

children.label: Pull up the stories
children.note: 3.1 or 3.2 or 3.3 raises a list - the Google keepers pull per section or query and keep nothing, the Feedly keepers open what 2 built. 3.4 only where the surface offers filters, and vLA0 round-trips every one before a single range sticks. 3.5 on every list; 3.6 where the surface clusters outlets; 3.7 on the newsroom service. re-entered per query - three searches in a row (64Vu).

questions.question: Does the page offer mute filters?
questions.why: The screen offers a 'GET MUTE FILTERS' button designed to remove irrelevant articles and fine-tune the news feed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to permanently customize their feed by filtering out specific unwanted keywords.
questions.check: Does the page offer mute filters, and are they part of a paid plan?
questions.say_example: The site offered mute filters - didn't touch them

questions.question: Which sidebar tab is active, the algorithmic For-you or the followed one?
questions.why: The left sidebar displays distinct navigation options like 'For you' and 'Following', which dictate whether you see algorithmically suggested news or topics you have explicitly chosen.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to leverage your personally curated feeds to quickly locate topics you already track.
questions.check: Which sidebar tab is active, the algorithmic one or the followed one?
questions.say_example: The <For you> tab is Google picking stories for you. You asked for your topics, so I'm using <Following>.

questions.question: What topics, locations, and sources are you currently following?
questions.why: Reviewing the empty state messages under the 'Topics & Sources' tab confirms whether you have already set up quick access to the specific subject you want to read about.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the awareness of your account's current personalization state and the knowledge that no specific topics or sources are currently saved for quick access.
questions.check: Does the Topics & Sources tab show followed items or an empty state?
questions.say_example: You're not following anything here yet, so I'll search for the topic instead.

questions.question: Do you have any saved searches available?
questions.why: The screen displays an empty state message indicating no saved searches exist, meaning you must search for your topic manually instead of using a shortcut.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the awareness that their saved searches list is empty and the opportunity to manage their personalized news feed shortcuts.
questions.check: Does the saved-searches area list any saved searches?
questions.say_example: No saved searches on the account - searched fresh

questions.question: Which sidebar feed matches the asked topic?
questions.why: The expanded sidebar shows multiple marketing sources with unread counts, requiring a choice of which specific publication or author to prioritize.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to select a preferred industry expert or publication based on your personal trust and reading preferences.
questions.check: Which sidebar feed matches the asked topic, and what is its unread count?
questions.say_example: Opened the <EdTech> feed - <593> unread

questions.question: What topic do you want to search for?
questions.why: The search bar prompts for topics, locations, or sources, requiring you to specify the exact subject you want to read about.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to choose a news topic that aligns with your personal interests or immediate curiosity.
questions.check: Is the search box empty, with no topic named in the request?
questions.say_example: What news do you want to follow? A topic, a team, or a place all work.

questions.question: Does the results page heading show the searched topic?
questions.why: Confirming that the timeline updates to 'Health News' ensures the platform correctly processed your specific query.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means losing the ability to personally verify that the search results accurately reflect the exact topic you had in mind.
questions.check: Does the results page heading show the topic that was searched?
questions.say_example: I searched <health news>, but the page came back with <something else>. I'm running the search again.

questions.question: Did the search engine automatically alter your search term to a more common spelling or related topic?
questions.why: Platforms sometimes silently autocorrect niche or specific terms, displaying a 'Showing results for...' message and returning irrelevant articles.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to notice the unwanted correction and click 'Search instead for...' to force the exact query.
questions.check: Does the page say 'Showing results for' a different query than the one entered?
questions.say_example: The site changed your search to <red sox scores>. I'm putting it back to exactly what you asked.

questions.question: Did the site return zero results for your specific query, requiring you to check for typos or use broader terms?
questions.why: A highly specific or misspelled query might yield an empty state, forcing a pivot in the search strategy.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to realize their search was too narrow or misspelled and to manually adjust their approach.
questions.check: Does the results page show zero results or an empty state?
questions.say_example: Nothing came back for that. I'll try broader words.

children.label: Narrow the results
children.note: 3.4.1 first on a general engine. 3.4.2 to 3.4.4 in any order, each applied, inspected, and reverted before the next (vLA0) - only 3.4.5 sticks. 3.4.3 is also how the newsroom keeper reaches text advisories (AE9a).

questions.question: Are the current results old or from non-news sites?
questions.why: The screen showed outdated articles from May 2018 and non-news links like Wikipedia, meaning the default search results did not meet the requirement for recent news.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the control to decide whether to refine the search using built-in platform tools or by manually modifying the search keywords.
questions.check: Are the visible results old or from non-news sites like Wikipedia?
questions.say_example: These results are old, some from <2018>, and half aren't news. I'm switching to the news results and filtering to <this week>.

questions.question: Are you still on the 'News' tab for your search results?
questions.why: The screen shows the 'All' tab underlined in blue and a Wikipedia article as the top result, indicating general web results instead of news.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that the agent is actually looking at news articles rather than general web results.
questions.check: Which results tab is underlined as active?
questions.say_example: We're on the <All> tab, so these are web results. I'm switching to <News>.

questions.question: Which sort order is selected, date or relevance?
questions.why: The dropdown menu offers both 'Sorted by date' and 'Sorted by relevance', forcing a choice between seeing the absolute newest articles or the most topically accurate ones first.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide whether strict recency or topical relevance is more important for your specific news search.
questions.check: Which sort order is selected, date or relevance?
questions.say_example: Sorted by date, newest first

questions.question: Did your filter restrict the search results to only show blog posts?
questions.why: The first result displayed was a 2018 blog post, indicating that the current search parameters might be excluding authoritative recent news.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to notice that a filter is returning outdated blog content instead of actual news and decide to revert it.
questions.check: Are the top results blog posts rather than news articles?
questions.say_example: This filter left mostly <blog posts>, and the first is from <2018>. I'm taking it off.

questions.question: Which media-type checkboxes are selected in the filter?
questions.why: The screen displays checkboxes for 'Video' and 'Advisories', allowing you to remove unwanted media formats from the search results.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to specify your preferred media format for consuming the news.
questions.check: Which media-type checkboxes are selected in the filter?
questions.say_example: Filtered to <text advisories> - videos off

questions.question: Which time window is selected in the date filter?
questions.why: The dropdown offers multiple time frames like 'Past hour' or 'Past month', which determines how recent the news articles must be to appear in your results.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this choice means the agent might pick a time frame that is too broad or too narrow for your specific information needs.
questions.check: Which time window is selected in the date filter?
questions.say_example: Limited results to <past week>

questions.question: Did the filter return older articles?
questions.why: Seeing older dates like 2017 and 2013 on the search results confirms that the archive filter is functioning correctly.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the visual confirmation that the platform's date filters are actually working as intended before selecting an article.
questions.check: Do the dates on the results fall inside the chosen time window?
questions.say_example: The date filter didn't take. These results are from <2024>, and you asked for the <1990s>. I'm applying it again.

questions.question: Does the date filter match the years you entered?
questions.why: Verifying that the system expanded your input of '1990' and '1999' to the full calendar years ensures your search covers the entire intended timeframe.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to verify that the system's automatic date formatting perfectly aligns with their intended search boundaries.
questions.check: Does the applied filter chip show the full years that were entered?
questions.say_example: Date filter reads <Jan 1 1990 - Dec 31 1999>

questions.question: Is the top search result visually marked as 'Sponsored' or an ad rather than an organic news story?
questions.why: Search engines and aggregators place visually distinct but subtly labeled advertisements above organic news results, which can look identical to real articles.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to bypass paid placements and ensure they are selecting independent, relevant news coverage rather than commercial content.
questions.check: Is the top result labeled Sponsored or Ad?
questions.say_example: The top result is an ad, so I'm skipping it.

questions.question: Do the article timestamps actually match the 'Today' filter?
questions.why: The interface suggests the content is from today, but the visible timestamps reveal articles ranging from 17 hours to 5 days old.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance of getting truly recent news if the agent blindly trusts the category label instead of verifying the actual publication dates.
questions.check: Do the article timestamps fall within the period the active filter claims?
questions.say_example: The page says <Today>, but some of these are up to <5 days> old. The newest real one is <17 hours> old.

questions.question: Is the most recent article flagged as 'Opinion', 'Analysis', or 'Sponsored' rather than hard news?
questions.why: News aggregators and sites often interleave subjective commentary or paid content with chronological news, which might not serve the goal of finding factual updates.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the personal judgment to skip over editorials or ads in favor of objective reporting on the topic.
questions.check: Is the newest item labeled Opinion, Analysis, or Sponsored?
questions.say_example: The newest one is marked <Opinion>, so it's commentary. The newest actual news story is from <Reuters>, <2 hours> ago.

questions.question: Does the article show an original publish date older than its updated timestamp?
questions.why: Publishers sometimes update old articles, changing the timestamp to 'Just now' even though the core news is days or weeks old.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to notice that the content itself is stale despite the fresh timestamp.
questions.check: Does the article show an original publish date older than its updated timestamp?
questions.say_example: This one says <2 hours ago>, but that's just an update. The story itself is from <March>.

questions.question: Does the news item feature a 'Live' badge or pulsing visual indicator showing it is a developing story?
questions.why: Breaking news often features a distinct red or pulsing visual badge indicating that the page is actively updating with new information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the crucial context that the information is currently unfolding and that staying on the page will yield real-time updates.
questions.check: Does the item show a Live badge?
questions.say_example: This one is live and still updating. What's on the page now may change.

children.label: Compare the outlets on a story

questions.question: Does the story card offer a Full Coverage view with more outlets?
questions.why: The news card features a 'Full Coverage' button alongside related links from different publishers, offering a way to expand on the main headline.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to spontaneously decide how deeply they want to explore a specific news event based on the available sources.
questions.check: Does the story card offer a Full Coverage view, and how many outlets does it list?
questions.say_example: Full Coverage available - <6> outlets on this story

children.label: Check the advisories for coming footage

questions.question: What delivery time and content does the advisory pane list for the upcoming footage?
questions.why: The details pane on the right reveals the specific description and expected delivery time for the upcoming news.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to know exactly when the upcoming news footage will become available.
questions.check: What delivery time and content does the advisory pane list for the upcoming item?
questions.say_example: That footage isn't out yet. The advisory says it lands <today at 14:00 GMT>.

children.label: Read the story
children.note: 4.1 from any list; 4.2, then 4.3 when the preview runs out - four reads finish on the source site, two stay in the preview. 4.4 for video items. 4.5 closes the loop every time, by whichever door the surface gives.

questions.question: Is the opened article primarily a photo gallery or interactive infographic rather than standard text?
questions.why: A sighted user instantly recognizes when an article's main content is visual (like a slideshow), which drastically changes how it is consumed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the warning that the content requires visual browsing, which is frustrating if they are relying on text-to-speech or a screen reader.
questions.check: Is the article body a photo gallery, slideshow, or infographic rather than text?
questions.say_example: This one is mostly pictures, a gallery of <20> photos with short captions. Want me to go through them?

questions.question: Which of these recent business articles do you want to open?
questions.why: The screen displays the 'Latest' business tab with articles from 5 to 6 hours ago, providing the necessary options to select and open a current story.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the chance to personally pick the specific business headline that most appeals to their current interests.
questions.check: Which recent articles does the list show, with source and age?
questions.say_example: Three fresh ones. <Reuters>, <5 hours> ago, on <the earnings call>. <AP>, <6 hours>, on <the layoffs>. Which one should I open?

questions.question: Does the content of the opened article match the preview snippet from the search results?
questions.why: Verifying that the article text matches the preview snippet ensures you have opened the correct article.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user receives incorrect information if the agent opens an article that doesn't match the expected content from the search results.
questions.check: Does the opened article's text contain the snippet shown in the results?
questions.say_example: This page doesn't match the story I clicked. I'm going back to pick it again.

questions.question: Is the full article text visible, or cut off with a link to the source site?
questions.why: The screen showed the title and subtitle, but the author's name and the rest of the text were cut off.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user misses the actual news content if the agent stops before the article fully loads.
questions.check: Is the full article text visible, or does it cut off with a link to the source site?
questions.say_example: Feedly only has the first paragraph. I'm opening the full story on <the Guardian>.

questions.question: Are you currently viewing the opened article or still browsing the aggregator's feed?
questions.why: The screen shows the active tab is the Guardian article, contradicting the claim that the aggregator feed is being scrolled.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses accurate tracking of whether the agent has successfully opened the target article or is still searching the feed.
questions.check: Which tab is active, the article or the aggregator feed?
questions.say_example: On the <Guardian> article tab

questions.question: Does a sign-up or consent pop-up cover the article text?
questions.why: News sites aggressively overlay the content with consent forms or email capture pop-ups that must be navigated before the article is visible.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over what data they consent to sharing or whether they want to subscribe to the publisher's mailing list just to read one article.
questions.check: Does a sign-up or consent pop-up cover the article text?
questions.say_example: A sign-up pop-up is covering the story. I closed it without giving your email.

questions.question: Did the link from the aggregator lead to a 404 error or a removed page on the publisher's site?
questions.why: Aggregators sometimes index articles that are subsequently taken down or moved by the original publisher, resulting in a broken link.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the awareness that the selected source is unavailable and the chance to pick the next best article.
questions.check: Does the page show a 404 or article-removed message?
questions.say_example: That link is dead. The story was taken down, so I'll find it from another outlet.

questions.question: Does the page show a paywall or subscription prompt instead of the article?
questions.why: Clicking through to an original source often leads to a subscription prompt or paywall instead of the full text, forcing you to abandon the page and find a different source.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The ability to recognize an access barrier on the external site and decide to back out and choose a freely available article instead.
questions.check: Does the page show a paywall or subscription prompt instead of the article?
questions.say_example: The full story is behind a paywall at <the Journal>. I'll find the same story on a free site.

questions.question: Does the video playing in the pop-up match the news article you intended to open?
questions.why: Clicking the video thumbnail opens a pop-up player, making it necessary to confirm the video actually covers the specific news topic you selected.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the immediate visual confirmation that the pop-up video is the correct news story rather than an unrelated clip or ad.
questions.check: Does the video player's title match the story that was selected?
questions.say_example: This video doesn't match the story you picked. I'm closing it and opening the right one.

children.label: Save and curate the stories
children.note: 5.1 before the first save. 5.2 or 5.3 - 5.4 inside 5.3 on a first board. 5.5 after a save: the same check succeeds in one keeper and comes back empty in another. 5.6 then 5.7 only in the keeper that unwinds its own work (xbgg).

children.label: Review the save and share options

questions.question: Which save and share actions does the toolbar offer?
questions.why: The action bar displays numerous options like saving to a board, emailing, or sharing to social media, offering ways to retain or distribute the information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to organically decide to save or share an interesting article to your personal networks or reading lists.
questions.check: Which save and share actions does the toolbar offer?
questions.say_example: Toolbar offers save, email, and share - used save only

questions.question: Does the page show a read-later save control next to the article?
questions.why: The screen displayed a "Read Later" bookmark icon next to the article, offering the option to save it.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to curate a reading list of interesting articles for future reference.
questions.check: Does the page show a read-later save control next to the article?
questions.say_example: I'm saving this one to Read Later.

children.label: Save the story to a board

questions.question: Which board does the save dialog show the article going to?
questions.why: The star icon opens a modal to organize saved articles by project or topic, letting you create a custom board to easily find the article again.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally name the board and define the organizational structure for your saved news.
questions.check: Which board does the save dialog show the article going to?
questions.say_example: I'm saving this one to your <Research> board.

questions.question: Does the page ask for a name for the new board?
questions.why: The screen displays a 'Board name' popup that requires a custom text entry to organize the saved article.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent might choose a generic board name that does not fit your personal organizational system.
questions.check: Does the page ask for a name for the new board?
questions.say_example: The save needs a board. I'm making one called <Red Sox>. Say a different name if you want one.

questions.question: Is the article you saved earlier visible in the Read Later section?
questions.why: The screen displays 'No Read Later Stories Yet', indicating that the article you attempted to save earlier was not successfully added to the list.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose access to the specific article you intended to read because the agent moves on to a different section instead of verifying why the save action failed.
questions.check: Does the Read Later list show the article that was saved?
questions.say_example: The save didn't stick. Read Later is still empty, so I'm saving it again.

children.label: Remove the story from the board

questions.question: Are you sure you want to delete the entire board?
questions.why: The '...' dropdown menu displays both harmless sorting options like 'Latest' and the destructive 'Delete' option, requiring careful selection.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to prevent the permanent deletion of their curated board if the agent mistakenly chooses the wrong menu item.
questions.check: Does the menu show a delete option for this board, and what is the board's name?
questions.say_example: This deletes the whole <Research> board and everything saved on it. Sure?

children.label: Download and import the footage
children.note: 6.1, then 6.2 and 6.3 in the browser, 6.4 to 6.6 in the editor, 6.7 when playback stutters. one keeper runs it (AE9a), and the task ends with the transcode still at 12 percent.

questions.question: Which specific search result should you select from the list?
questions.why: The results show multiple recent items with different media types and topics, such as a video about Russian ice hockey versus one about India's IOC ban, requiring a choice based on relevance.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to personally select the specific sub-topic and media format that best fits your current interest.
questions.check: Which results does the list show, with media type and date?
questions.say_example: Two match. A <video> from <today> on <the hockey team>, and an <article> from <yesterday>. Which one do you want?

questions.question: Does this video and its accompanying transcript contain the specific footage and story details you need?
questions.why: Checking the video player and the text sections like 'SHOWS:' and 'STORY:' confirms whether the asset actually contains the relevant footage and information about the Russian hockey team.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally watch the video and read the transcript to ensure the footage and story nuances meet your exact expectations.
questions.check: Do the SHOWS and STORY sections describe the footage that was asked for?
questions.say_example: The script says this video shows <the arena outside> only. It doesn't have <the game footage> you need, so I'll keep looking.

questions.question: Which files does the download menu have selected by default?
questions.why: The download menu defaults to including XML and other metadata, but selecting only the video file saves storage and bandwidth if you are writing your own story.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to prevent the agent from downloading unnecessary metadata files that clutter your local storage.
questions.check: Which files does the download menu have selected by default?
questions.say_example: The download comes with extra files, <XML and metadata>. I'm taking just the video.

children.label: Name the file and keep the extension

questions.question: What filename and extension does the save dialog show?
questions.why: The default filename is a cryptic string of characters, so renaming it and keeping the extension visible makes the file much easier to identify later.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to apply their own personal naming conventions and organizational preferences to downloaded files.
questions.check: What filename and extension does the save dialog show?
questions.say_example: Saved as <russia-hockey-dec18.mp4>

questions.question: Does the import dialog have the copy-to-library option selected?
questions.why: The import settings dialog requires deciding whether to copy files to the local events folder to prevent losing access if the original drive is disconnected.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over their local file management and the assurance that media is safely stored on their primary hard drive.
questions.check: Does the import dialog have the copy-to-library option selected?
questions.say_example: I'm telling it to copy the files into your library. That way they still play if the drive is unplugged.

children.label: Place the clip on the timeline

questions.question: What progress does the Background Tasks window show for the import?
questions.why: The Background Tasks window shows the media import is at 12%, which helps determine how much longer the process will take.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to monitor the exact progress of the background import and decide whether to wait for it to finish.
questions.check: What progress does the Background Tasks window show for the import?
questions.say_example: Import at <12%> in Background Tasks

questions.question: Does the Background Tasks window show the media still transcoding?
questions.why: The screen showed choppy playback of a high-resolution file, which prompted an investigation into background tasks.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: A person delegating to an agent loses the ability to visually assess playback quality and intuitively troubleshoot system performance issues.
questions.check: Does the Background Tasks window show the media still transcoding?
questions.say_example: The video may look choppy for a bit. It's still processing, at <12%>.

children.label: Close the session
children.note: 7.1 then 7.2. one keeper does both (v4vm); the rest stop the recorder or just stop.

questions.question: Did you log out of the account?
questions.why: The screen displays a promotional landing page with a 'LOGIN' button, confirming that the active session has ended.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that their personal account was securely closed and their session data protected at the end of the task.
questions.check: Does the page now show a login button instead of the account?
questions.say_example: The logout didn't take, you still look signed in. I'm trying again.
